methodological_rigor.justification: This nationwide retrospective administrative data study from the Helios hospital network (78 hospitals, n=20,005) employs generalized linear mixed models with hospital as a random factor — an appropriate approach to account for clustering. Standardized comorbidity (Elixhauser Comorbidity Index) and frailty (Hospital Frailty Risk Score) indices are validated tools applied from ICD-10 codes. The pre-pandemic vs. pandemic period comparison is a natural quasi-experiment but not a true controlled study. Key limitations include the administrative data nature (no tumor grading, functional status, or long-term outcomes), inability to establish causal relationships, potential coding errors, and the confounding effect of COVID-19 pandemic effects on health-seeking behavior which complicates interpretation of secular trends.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This large observational cohort study provides real-world evidence on age-specific trends in brain tumor care across a 7-year period at a nationally representative German hospital network. The identification of the 75–84 age bracket as uniquely not improving in comorbidity, frailty, or surgery rates is clinically actionable — this group may require targeted supportive care pathway development. However, the study is primarily descriptive, does not include tumor histology or survival data, and the pandemic comparison framework limits inference about true secular trends versus COVID-specific effects.

reporting_quality.justification: The manuscript follows STROBE conventions for observational studies: study setting and data source are described, inclusion/exclusion criteria and outcome definitions are clear, and statistical methods including the GLMM approach are detailed. However, some key reporting elements are incomplete: the administrative data coding procedures are briefly described but not validated against clinical records, the precise N per age bracket per phase is not presented, and interaction analyses testing whether pre-to-pandemic changes differ across frailty groups are mentioned but not fully reported. Data are institutional administrative records and are not publicly deposited.

novelty_literature.justification: This study builds on the authors' prior publication (Hong et al., 2023) by adding age-stratified and tumor-type-stratified analyses to the nationwide German brain tumor care dataset. The identification of the 75–84 year age group as uniquely resistant to the broader improvement trends observed in all other age groups is a novel granular finding. The comparison of trends across elderly age brackets and tumor types in a large nationwide cohort adds genuine value to the neuro-oncology literature, though the study is largely descriptive and the pandemic design limits generalizability of conclusions about secular trends.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is adequately written and organized with clear section headings and appropriate tables and figures. The discussion provides reasonable interpretations of the age-specific findings. However, some sections are repetitive (abstract, introduction, and results cover similar ground with limited added interpretation), and the discussion over-relies on speculative explanations for the 75–84 age bracket anomaly without sufficient data to support them. The statistical analysis section is somewhat dense and could benefit from clearer presentation of the key model results.

key_strengths: Large nationwide real-world cohort (n=20,005 across 78 German hospitals) providing representative data on temporal trends in brain tumor care across age groups — one of the largest such datasets for this question

Novel finding that the 75–84 year age bracket is uniquely resistant to the improved comorbidity, frailty, and surgical rates observed across all other age groups, with potential implications for targeted pathway development
Validated comorbidity (ECI) and frailty (HFRS) scoring tools applied appropriately from administrative data with GLMMs accounting for hospital clustering
key_concerns: Administrative data without tumor grading, histology, functional status, or long-term survival outcomes severely limits the clinical interpretability and actionability of the findings

The pandemic vs. pre-pandemic comparison conflates COVID-specific effects (healthcare avoidance, deferred referrals) with genuine secular trends in care, making it impossible to separate these effects without a COVID-naive comparator
The age-bracket anomaly in 75–84 year patients is described but not explained with sufficient evidence — the explanations offered (urgency of malignant tumors in this age group) remain speculative
As a secondary analysis of a previously published dataset (Hong et al., 2023), incremental novelty is limited and the contribution beyond the prior publication should be more clearly articulated
chief_reviewer.rationale: This descriptive nationwide administrative study adds useful age-stratified granularity to prior work on German brain tumor care trends and identifies a clinically interesting anomaly in the 75–84 year group. However, the lack of clinical outcome data, pandemic-confounded temporal comparison, and primarily descriptive scope place it at Tier 3; minor revisions addressing the novelty relative to the prior publication and more complete reporting of GLMM results are warranted.
